newsitem.title: INDIA: Dizzying array of outcomes in India crisis.
newsitem.headline: Dizzying array of outcomes in India crisis.

text.p: A standoff between India's ruling coalition and its new rival, the Congress party, has opened up a myriad of political possibilities with no guarantee the leader of either faction will prevail.
Erstwhile allies, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Congress chief Sitaram Kesri are locked in confrontation before a confidence vote in parliament on April 11.

Neither Deve Gowda's 15-party United Front alliance nor Congress wants to risk mid-term polls that opinion surveys indicate would strengthen the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), already parliament's biggest party.

But neither the United Front nor Congress has budged from irreconcilable positions since Kesri triggered the political crisis on March 30 by unexpectedly withdrawing his party's vital support for Deve Gowda.
Kesri has launched highly personal attacks on Deve Gowda and demanded he be removed.
"Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda should step down to facilitate commencement of dialogue between the Congress and the United Front," Kesri said on Tuesday.
The United Front, which chose Deve Gowda as its leader last June after as many as three others turned down the job, says it cannot submit to Congress's demands.

Waiting in the wings is the BJP, which held power for 12 days last May after inconclusive general elections but which failed to muster a majority when the United Front and Congress joined hands against the right-wing Hindu nationalists.

The three main groupings are far short of an outright parliamentary majority of 272 members. The BJP and its allies control 193 votes in the 542-member lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha. The United Front has 180, and Congress 140.
Senior politicians from the United Front and Congress have been shuttling across New Delhi for 10 days in search of a face-saving solution, but failed to break the logjam.
Rhetoric emanating from Congress and the BJP would appear to point to a massive defeat for Deve Gowda on the floor of the Lok Sabha, forcing him to resign.
In that case, President Shankar Dayal Sharma could ask either the BJP or Congress to try to form a government. If they failed, elections would ensue.
But Deve Gowda could resign before the confidence vote, as BJP leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee did in May.
This could pave the way for another United Front leader to take power with Congress's backing, or for Congress to take over -- perhaps without Kesri in charge.

The prime minister could recommend to the president that the Lok Sabha be dissolved, but that course would presuppose support in the United Front for fresh elections. What is more, politicians say the president does not want snap polls.
To win the vote, Deve Gowda would need a simple majority of those present and voting. If the BJP abstained, he could easily win.

The BJP has kept its options open, and some politicians say the Hindu party would prefer to leave Deve Gowda in power to allow differences between the United Front and Congress to fester -- improving the BJP's chances of winning the next polls.
